original.title: An Integrative Theory of Intergroup Conflict

core_idea: Part of who we are comes from the groups we belong to. People sort themselves and others into groups, take on the group as part of their self-concept, and compare their group with others. Because a positive group identity supports self-esteem, people tend to favour their own group, even when groups are formed on trivial grounds.
key_concepts_note: Use the concepts already stored for this theory in the library (theories.concepts).
when_to_use: How do students, employees or citizens identify with a group (ethnic, national, professional, organizational), and how does that shape behaviour?
Why do in-group favouritism, stereotyping or intergroup tension appear?
How do lower-status groups respond to their position (mobility, creativity, competition)?
Typical data: surveys with identification scales, experiments, interviews about belonging and comparison.
common_mistakes: Treating any mention of 'identity' as social identity theory. The theory is about group membership and intergroup comparison.
Assuming identification always leads to hostility towards out-groups. The theory predicts favouritism, not necessarily conflict.
Blending social identity theory and self-categorization theory without saying which claims come from which.
